channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The US personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.4% year on year in August, below the market expectation of 3.7%, and core PCE rose 3%, below the expected 3.3%, lowering market expectations of an October rate rise.
item.description:
Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.2% from July, below the expected 0.3%, Commercial Times reports. After the release, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed about a 38% probability of a quarter-point rate rise in October, down from roughly 51% in the previous session and nearly 71% a week earlier, MarketScreener reports, and Goldman Sachs pushed its forecast for the next rise to December. POLITICO reports that the 3.4% headline rate remains above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Commercial Times also reports that the 30-year Treasury yield rose to 5.648%, its highest since 2002, while the two-year yield fell. The reporting does not give the energy component of the index or explain why long-term yields rose while the two-year yield fell.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The data lower the near-term odds of a further US rate rise but do not remove it: inflation remains well above target, and the 30-year Treasury yield rose to its highest since 2002 after the release. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise in long-term yields while short-term yields fall raises the cost of long-term financing for housing and capital investment even when the central bank holds, which matters for construction and industrial customers more than the policy rate alone. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US construction and capital-goods customers are the segments most sensitive to long-term rates. Points that may be worth considering include how US customers' investment and building plans respond to long-term yields at their highest since 2002, and what a Fed decision at the end of October could change.

Commercial Times | MarketScreener | POLITICO

item.title: The US economy grew at a 2.2% annual rate in the second quarter, revised up from the previous estimate of 1.5%, the Commerce Department says, with consumer spending up at a 3.8% rate and business investment excluding housing at 9%.
item.description:
Consumer spending, which accounts for around 70% of US economic activity, rose at a 3.8% annual rate in the quarter against 0.7% in the first quarter, The Economic Times reports; MarketScreener reports the consumer-spending figure was revised up from 3.4%. Business investment excluding housing rose at a 9% rate, reflecting spending linked to artificial intelligence, and a measure of underlying growth excluding government spending and trade grew at a 4.6% rate, up from 1.8% in the first quarter. According to MarketScreener, about half of the upward revision came from consumption and half from private investment, and first-quarter growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%; measured from the income side, growth was 2.6%. MarketScreener also reports that the growth numbers suggest the economy has so far held up against headwinds from the war with Iran, helped by AI investment and tax refunds. The reporting does not give revised figures for housing or manufacturing output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The revision shows US demand in the second quarter stronger than first reported, led by consumers and by AI-related investment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth led by technology investment and household spending supports demand for electronics, data-centre construction and consumer goods more than for traditional heavy industry, and stronger growth also supports the case for higher interest rates that markets are weighing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the US is a major market in which construction, electronics and consumer-goods packaging all depend on this demand. Points that may be worth considering include whether the strength in the second quarter has carried into the third, and how higher rates could affect housing-related demand.

The Economic Times | MarketScreener | MarketScreener

item.title: S&P Global's South Korea manufacturing PMI rose to 53.9 in September from 52.3, its highest since May, and Taiwan's PMI reached 56.7 from 54.7, while Japan's fell to 54.1 from 54.9, the slowest growth in six months.
item.description:
Factory activity across Asia generally expanded in September, driven by the artificial intelligence boom, with manufacturing in export economies such as Taiwan, South Korea and Japan supported by strong demand for chips and AI-related products, Commercial Times reports. South Korea's factory activity grew at its fastest pace in four months, and its index has stayed above the 50 line that separates expansion from contraction for the tenth consecutive month. In Japan the slowdown came from slower growth in output and new orders. The reporting does not give figures for China, India or the ASEAN economies in this release, or any sector breakdown beyond the reference to chips and AI-related products. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The indices are purchasing managers' surveys, not measurements of output volume. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, growth concentrated in chips and AI-related products means demand in East Asian manufacturing is uneven between electronics and other industries, and the readings sit alongside the August sales and production declines at Japan's eight major carmakers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics assembly in Taiwan and South Korea is the segment these surveys point to. Points that may be worth considering include how orders from electronics and semiconductor-packaging customers in Taiwan and South Korea compare with those from automotive and general industry in the region.

Commercial Times

item.title: China's express delivery volume exceeded 150 billion parcels as of 29 September, 12 days earlier than in 2025, according to the State Post Bureau, after the country handled 198.95 billion parcels in 2025, up 13.6% year on year.
item.description:
The figure was reported by China Daily and Global Times, citing the State Post Bureau. The reporting does not give a year-on-year growth rate for 2026 so far, the split between domestic and cross-border parcels, the weight or value of the shipments, or any breakdown by packaging type.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The data describe express delivery volume reaching 150 billion parcels earlier than in 2025, and a parcel count measures deliveries, not packaging material consumption. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, each parcel involves corrugated boxes, mailer bags, labels and sealing tapes, so parcel volume is one of the drivers of demand for paper-based and flexible packaging and for the adhesives used in box making, labelling and closing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, e-commerce packaging in China is a high-volume end use where parcel numbers are one driver of demand. Points that may be worth considering include how packaging customers in China are planning for parcel volume growth, and whether parcel growth translates into demand for case-sealing and labelling materials in the coming peak season.

China Daily | Global Times

item.title: The French government has extended aid to chemical sectors facing higher electricity costs from greenhouse-gas quotas passed on by power producers, with an envelope of EUR 150 million, France Chimie Ile-de-France reports.
item.description:
Electricity producers are subject to greenhouse-gas quotas and pass the cost of those quotas on in the electricity price, which raises electricity costs for the chemical sectors concerned and can lead to "carbon leakage", a risk of relocation because of the price effect, according to France Chimie Ile-de-France. The government has extended the aid to these sectors with an exceptional envelope of EUR 150 million. The report does not name the eligible chemical sectors or companies, give the period covered, say how the aid is calculated, or compare the envelope with previous years. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The decision is a support measure for indirect carbon costs, not a change in carbon pricing itself: it addresses the cost of quotas passed on in the electricity price for the sectors concerned. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, such compensation is an instrument several EU states use for electricity-intensive industries, so its extent differs by country and can affect where electricity-intensive production is located. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the main exposure is through electricity-intensive suppliers of chemical raw materials in France, whose costs and location decisions the aid is designed to influence. Points that may be worth considering include whether French raw-material suppliers fall within the eligible sectors, and how compensation for indirect carbon costs compares across the EU countries where supplying or own production sites are located.

France Chimie Ile-de-France

item.title: Global sales of Japan's eight major carmakers fell 4.6% in August on a year earlier to 1,854,797 units, and their production in Japan fell 5.9% to 487,195 units, China Economic Net reports.
item.description:
Global production by the eight companies fell 4.1% year on year to 1,742,545 units in August, according to the report. Toyota's global sales fell 6.4% to 790,743 units and Honda's 9.2% to 263,015 units; Subaru's domestic sales fell 8.9% and its exports 14.4%, and Mitsubishi Motors' sales fell 8.7%. Suzuki's global sales rose 19.3%, which the report attributes to India lowering its goods and services tax, a tax equivalent to a consumption tax, which pulled up demand. The reporting does not give the reasons for the declines at the other carmakers, a regional breakdown of sales outside India, or comparisons with July. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are measured sales and production for named companies, and they show a broad decline in August, with Suzuki, whose growth the report links to India's tax cut, as the exception. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, falling domestic production in Japan reduces material consumption at Japanese assembly and component plants directly, while growth tied to a tax cut in India can fade once the effect of the cut has passed. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japanese carmakers are customers both in Japan and at their plants abroad, so the regional pattern of their output matters as much as the total. Points that may be worth considering include whether the decline at Toyota and Honda reflects Japan, the US or China, and how far demand at Japanese carmakers' Indian operations is tied to the tax change.

China Economic Net

item.title: BMW Group is investing around EUR 2 billion in car and battery production in Germany to strengthen its earning power, and will reduce the number of business units and associated management positions by 20% by mid-2027 in a reorganisation.
item.description:
The report places the move among German carmakers' efforts to strengthen profitability under pressure from the transition to electric vehicles, global supply problems, high energy prices and fierce competition from China. BMW aims to raise profitability by streamlining its model range, shortening development times and working more closely with suppliers, according to the report. The group also plans to reduce the number of model variants and to make more use of artificial intelligence, for example in crash-test simulations and driver-assistance systems. The reporting does not name the plants that will receive the investment, its timing, or the split between vehicle and battery production, and it does not give the number of employees affected by the reduction in management positions. It does not report job cuts beyond those management positions. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The investment and the reorganisation point in the same direction: investment in German vehicle and battery production, combined with fewer model variants and closer work with suppliers. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, fewer variants usually mean fewer material specifications and larger volumes per specification, and shorter development times put weight on suppliers that can qualify materials quickly and support simulation-based development. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, battery production and body assembly in Germany are applications where structural bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials are specified. Points that may be worth considering include which German BMW sites and battery lines the investment reaches, how a reduced variant count could change approved material lists, and what "working more closely with suppliers" may mean for qualification and pricing.

Yahoo! - Germany

item.title: Floods in Bangkok have suspended operations at companies since last week, with flights at Suvarnabhumi Airport not expected to resume until 4 October and Thai Airways suspending cargo acceptance from 1 to 6 October.
item.description:
Continuous heavy rain on low-lying terrain flooded Bangkok, and companies have successively suspended operations since last week, Commercial Times reports, citing local Taiwanese businesses, which say PCB, thermal-solution and AI-assembly plants around Bangkok have all been affected to varying degrees; the supply chain expects shipments to be hit, potentially affecting the September revenue of listed companies with factories there. Thai Airways announced a suspension of cargo acceptance for 1–6 October after flooding prevented staff from reaching work and left goods awaiting delivery or transfer, The Nation reports; the Transport Ministry has intervened to keep import and export warehouse services open and would coordinate additional personnel, while freight acceptance could slow to match handling capacity, and Airports of Thailand was asked to allocate temporary space for stranded cargo. Lianhe Zaobao reports some Bangkok restaurants losing up to 80% of revenue as traffic disruption cut diners and supply disruption pushed up ingredient prices. The reporting does not give the number of plants or companies affected, the length of the companies' suspensions, or an estimate of losses for the floods in Bangkok.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reporting describes an event in progress with dated operating effects on air freight and on electronics manufacturing in the Bangkok area. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a suspension of air-cargo acceptance at a regional hub delays high-value, time-sensitive components first, and electronics assembly chains built around just-in-time deliveries tend to feel such interruptions beyond the flooded area itself. On the same general reading, Thailand is also a regional base for automotive and electrical manufacturing, so a longer disruption could reach customers in those industries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, both deliveries into Thai electronics and assembly plants and the shipments out of them are exposed while freight acceptance could slow to match handling capacity. Points that may be worth considering include which customer plants and logistics routes around Bangkok are affected, whether air shipments can be moved to sea freight or other airports, and how quickly operations restart after 6 October.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | The Nation - Thailand | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: India has notified the CAFE-III rules, under which the fuel-consumption benchmark for passenger vehicle fleets tightens from 3.996 litres per 100 km in FY28 to 3.3273 litres in FY32.
item.description:
The rules apply progressively over five years starting in April 2027, The Economic Times reports. The target line has been flattened to give relatively softer targets for lighter vehicles and tighter requirements for heavier ones, the reference weight has been raised by 13.6% from 1,082 kg to 1,229 kg, and the list of recognised fuel-conservation technologies has grown from four to 12. Battery EVs count three times in the fleet-average calculation, Business Standard reports, as do qualifying range-extender EVs, and biofuel vehicles receive separate carbon-neutrality factors — 22.3% for flex-fuel ethanol vehicles, 8% for eligible E20-and-above petrol vehicles including strong hybrids and plug-in hybrids, and at least 5% for CNG vehicles, The Hindu Business Line reports. Non-compliant companies will face debits that can be traded or bought, according to The Economic Times. Business Standard reports the framework could push carmakers towards smaller, cheaper EVs while potentially making larger petrol and diesel cars more expensive, and industry executives it quotes say it strengthens the case for affordable EVs that can generate higher volumes. The reporting does not give the penalty level for non-compliance or the current fleet average of individual carmakers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rules are a notified regulation with dated targets, and the shift in product mix reported by Business Standard and The Economic Times is an expectation in the press, supported by executives' comments, not yet a measured change. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, fleet fuel-efficiency targets usually raise the value of weight reduction and of electrified powertrains, both of which change the materials used in body, battery and interior assemblies, and the flatter, weight-sensitive target line affects heavier vehicles most. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, India's car market is an end-market where bonding of lighter structures and of battery systems could gain in relevance as carmakers plan for 2027–2032. Points that may be worth considering include which Indian and foreign carmakers in India are likely to change powertrain and vehicle-weight plans first, and how the credit for hybrids and flex-fuel vehicles alters the expected mix between EVs and combustion vehicles.

The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line - India | Business Standard - India | The Economic Times

item.title: Prices of 3,153 food and beverage items in Japan are set to rise in October, according to Teikoku Databank, which attributes the increases to higher packaging costs stemming from the Middle East conflict and a weaker yen.
item.description:
The October count follows 4,965 items whose prices were raised in September, and brings the number of food and beverage items that have seen or are scheduled to see price rises in 2026 to 20,187, above 20,000 for the second consecutive year, The Straits Times and Japan Today report, citing the Teikoku Databank survey. By category, alcoholic and other beverages account for the largest number of October price rises at 1,399 items, followed by seasonings at 820 and processed foods at 668. The Straits Times adds that the October increases extend to dining out, leisure and utility bills following the end of government subsidies. The reporting does not give the size of the price rises, the share of the increases attributed to packaging as against the yen or other costs, which packaging materials have become more expensive, or how many items Teikoku tracks in total.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The survey names packaging cost as a cause of consumer price rises, which places an effect of the Middle East conflict at the end of the food supply chain. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, packaging films, laminates, labels and closures are largely made from petrochemical inputs, so higher oil and naphtha prices reach food and beverage brand owners through their packaging suppliers, and brand owners passing costs on to consumers can in turn press packaging converters to find savings. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, laminating, labelling and case-sealing adhesives are part of that packaging cost base. Points that may be worth considering include whether Japanese and other Asian packaging customers are seeking price relief, down-gauging or material changes, and how far packaging-related cost increases in food and beverages are being accepted by retailers elsewhere.

The Straits Times | Japan Today

item.title: EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen says the EU has spent around EUR 100 billion more to import the same amount of fossil fuels since the Iran war broke out at the end of February.
item.description:
Jørgensen gave the figure as EU energy ministers prepared to discuss, at a meeting in Dublin on 29 September, how to respond to the likely continuation of high energy prices this winter, according to Beijing Daily. He urged member states to study measures to reduce energy demand, to take targeted temporary measures to stabilise prices, and to continue replenishing natural gas stocks. In Dublin he also said he had sent a "very clear signal" to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright that a US ban on diesel exports would not be in anyone's interest, Yahoo Taiwan reports. FAZ reports that since the start of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a barrel of oil at times cost almost USD 120, almost twice the pre-war level, and gas sometimes more than EUR 80 per megawatt hour, an increase of 150%, and that the higher gas price also makes industrial products such as fertilisers more expensive. The reporting does not break the EUR 100 billion down by fuel or member state, give the volumes or the baseline prices used, or report what the ministers decided in Dublin.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figure measures cost, not volume: it describes the same imports bought at higher prices, so it measures a higher import bill, not a change in volume. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a bill of this size feeds through to European industry mainly via gas and electricity prices and the price of oil-based raw materials, and the commissioner's call to study demand-reduction measures and take targeted temporary price measures points to a winter in which policy choices, not only markets, shape energy costs. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, both energy for production and petrochemical raw materials sit in this chain. Points that may be worth considering include which European sites and raw materials carry the most exposure to gas and oil prices this winter, and whether national demand-reduction or price measures could apply to industrial users.

Bjd.com.cn | Yahoo! - Taiwan | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Sentiment in the German chemical industry improved again in September, with expectations positive for the first time in over a year, but new orders have been falling again since the summer, ChemEurope reports.
item.description:
According to ChemEurope, for the second consecutive month a majority of German chemical companies rated their current business situation positively in September, and their expectations for the coming months turned positive again for the first time in more than a year, which the report links to an anticipated pickup in export business. The same report says there is still no sign of an independent and sustainable recovery: the wider economic upturn is supported mainly by government investment in infrastructure and defence, while private investment and industrial demand show initial signs of stabilisation at a low level. New orders from domestic and foreign markets began to decline again as early as the summer, production and sales have recently lost momentum, and about 40% of companies cite the lack of orders as a serious obstacle to business. The summary does not name the institute that ran the survey, give the index values or their change from August, break the results down by product segment, or give figures for production or sales. It rests on one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reading is a survey of sentiment, not a measurement of output: better expectations alongside falling orders describe companies that expect more business than they currently have. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, a recovery carried mainly by public infrastructure and defence spending tends to favour construction, transport and defence-related supply chains over consumer and general industrial demand, and German chemical producers are suppliers of raw materials to adhesive technologies as well as competitors for the same industrial customers. If the expected export pickup does not arrive, the order shortage the companies report would remain the binding constraint. Points that may be worth considering include whether orders from infrastructure and defence customers are developing differently from those of general industry, and how German raw-material suppliers' order books compare with their own improved expectations.

ChemEurope.Com
